title: Pseudomonas aeruginosa: Infections and novel approaches to treatment "Knowing the enemy" the threat of Pseudomonas aeruginosa and exploring novel approaches to treatment (Infect Med (Beijing). 2023;2(3):178-194)

claims.text: P. aeruginosa is a Gram-negative, motile, nonfermenting, rod-shaped (bacillus) bacterium.
claims.byte_quote: Pseudomonas aeruginosa is a motile, nonfermenting, Gram-negative, rod-shaped

claims.text: P. aeruginosa colonizes healthy people: isolated from the throat of 5% and stools of 3% of nonhospitalized patients.
claims.byte_quote: has also been isolated from the throat (5%) and stools (3%) of nonhospitalized patients

claims.text: P. aeruginosa is the 4th leading cause of HAIs, accounts for 20% of all HAIs in Europe/US, and is responsible for 75% of deaths of severely burnt patients.
claims.byte_quote: It is the fourth leading cause of hospital-associated infections (HAIs) and accounts for 20% of all HAIs in Europe and United States [45] and is responsible for 75% of all deaths of severely burnt patients [46].

claims.text: P. aeruginosa is the 2nd most common cause of ventilator-associated pneumonia in the US and ranks 3rd among catheter-associated UTIs.
claims.byte_quote: P. aeruginosa is the second most common cause of ventilator-associated pneumonia in the United States [43], and ranks third among urinary tract infections associated with catheters [44].

claims.text: P. aeruginosa causes 3%-7% of bloodstream infection cases, with 27%-48% morbidity/mortality in critically ill patients.
claims.byte_quote: The bacterium is responsible for 3%–7% of blood stream infection cases with high morbidity and mortality rates (27%–48%) in critically ill patients [125,126].

claims.text: P. aeruginosa is the 3rd most common Gram-negative cause of nosocomial bloodstream infection, accounting for 4.3% of all nosocomial BSI cases.
claims.byte_quote: reported P. aeruginosa as the third most common Gram-negative bacteria causing nosocomial BSI and accounted for 4.3% of all cases.

claims.text: Patients with burns and AIDS are more vulnerable to systemic (bloodstream) P. aeruginosa infection.
claims.byte_quote: Patients with burns and AIDs are more vulnerable to systemic infection by P. aeruginosa

claims.text: In adult neutropenic oncohematological patients (incl. HSCT recipients), P. aeruginosa BSI isolates were 25.4% MDR and 19.3% XDR.
claims.byte_quote: P. aeruginosa strains isolated from adult neutropenic oncohematological patients, including hematopoietic stem cell transplant recipients, were caused by multi drug resistant (25.4%) and extensively drug resistant bacteria (19.3%).

claims.text: P. aeruginosa is associated with 7%-12% of all nosocomial UTIs.
claims.byte_quote: associated with 7%–12% of all nosocomial urinary tract infections [44,127].

claims.text: P. aeruginosa UTIs usually follow catheterization or surgery (device/instrumentation risk factor).
claims.byte_quote: The bacterium usually causes UTIs following catheterization or surgery [75].

claims.text: P. aeruginosa UTI can progress to sepsis, fatal especially in older, immunocompromised, and diabetic patients.
claims.byte_quote: may cause complications such as sepsis that can be fatal in older patients, immunocompromised patients and individuals with diabetes [19].

claims.text: Burn wounds are first colonized by Gram-positive organisms (Staphylococcus aureus, Streptococcus pyogenes) before P. aeruginosa infection.
claims.byte_quote: Wounds first become colonized by Gram-positive organisms such as Staphylococcus aureus and Streptococcus pyogenes before infection by P. aeruginosa

claims.text: Source/portal associations: burn-wound infection arises from endogenous GI/upper-respiratory flora (causing septicaemia); bloodstream infections are nosocomial.
claims.byte_quote: Burn wound infectionEndogenous flora of the gastrointestinal and or upper respiratory tract [87,88]Septicaemia [46]Blood stream infectionsNosocomial [89]

claims.text: In India, carbapenem resistance among P. aeruginosa is high (40%-47%).
claims.byte_quote: A scoping report on antimicrobial resistance in India reported a high prevalence of carbapenem resistance among P. aeruginosa (40%–47%)

claims.text: DTR P. aeruginosa is non-susceptible to all of: piperacillin-tazobactam, ceftazidime, cefepime, aztreonam, meropenem, imipenem-cilastatin, ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin (the anti-pseudomonal drug list).
claims.byte_quote: DTR is described in this guidance as P. aeruginosa that does not display sensitivity to any of the following drugs: piperacillin-tazobactam, ceftazidime, cefepime, aztreonam, meropenem, imipenem-cilastatin, ciprofloxacin, and levofloxacin.

claims.text: P. aeruginosa causes bacterial keratitis in 6%-39% of cases in the USA and 8%-21% in south India (contact-lens/ocular-surgery risk).
claims.byte_quote: P. aeruginosa is responsible for causing bacterial keratitis in 6% to 39% of the cases in the USA [116,117] and 8% to 21% in south India [116].

claims.text: P. aeruginosa accounted for 17.5% of ventilator-associated pneumonia cases and 9.26% of hospital-associated pneumonia cases.
claims.byte_quote: P. aeruginosa accounted for 17.5% of all cases in ventilator-associated pneumonia and 9.26% of all cases in hospital-associated pneumonia [91].

claims.text: P. aeruginosa is implicated in 0.3%-11% of community-acquired pneumonia and 2.2%-20% of healthcare-associated pneumonia.
claims.byte_quote: Reported percentages of P. aeruginosa implicated in community-acquired pneumonia vary from 0.3% to 11%, whereas it varies from 2.2% to 20% in healthcare associated pneumonia [150,151].

claims.text: Hospitalized P. aeruginosa UTI patients had 17.7% mortality at 30 days and 33.9% at 90 days.
claims.byte_quote: reported 17.7% mortalities at 30 days and 33.9% mortalities at 90 days [130].

claims.text: P. aeruginosa was the 3rd most common Gram-negative uropathogen, causing 7.1% of nosocomial UTIs in the Asia-Pacific region (2009-2010).
claims.byte_quote: P. aeruginosa was found to be the third most common Gram-negative pathogen causing 7.1% of all nosocomial urinary tract infections in surveillance studies from the Asia-Pacific region in 2009 to 2010 [128].
